newsitem.title: USA: American, pilots talk as strike deadline looms.
newsitem.headline: American, pilots talk as strike deadline looms.

text.p: The top U.S. mediator overseeing the dispute between American Airlines and its pilots said on Thursday he was hopeful an agreement could be worked out in time to avert a strike at midnight on Friday (0500 GMT on Saturday).
"I am hopeful, and within the next hour I may be more optimistic," Kenneth Hipp, chairman of the National Mediation Board told reporters.
But a negotiator for the Allied Pilots' Association said the airline apparently had rejected the union's latest offer aimed at preventing a walkout that would ground the nation's No. 2 carrier.
"It's my understanding that the company has rejected it," said Brian Mayhew, chairman of APA's negotiating committee.
However, American Airlines president Donald Carty made no reference to such a rejection, saying only that the carrier had some concerns about the proposal.
"We have a long, long way to go and we have a short time to do it ... I'm not sure we're going to be able to differentiate between tonight and tomorrow morning," Carty said.
Hipp, who has been shuttling between the APA and the company, said he expected the two sides to meet face-to-face and also predicted negotiations could go throughout the night.

A strike would disrupt plans for hundreds of thousands of travelers. The Fort Worth, Texas-based airline is trying to rebook passengers on other carriers and has already canceled nearly all international flights scheduled for Friday night.

American Airlines spokesman John Hotard said on Thursday the carrier was cancelling 12 of its domestic flights scheduled for Friday. "There are some small domestic airports where we have no permanent place to park the planes if there is a strike, so we decided to cancel those 12 flights," he said.
A Transportation Department official said a strike could cost the U.S. economy up to $200 million a day.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the figure was contained in a government report sent to the National Mediation Board and the White House.

At the negotiations, the union said its proposal dealt with two of the key disputes with American -- pay for pilots on American's regular flights and whether its union pilots should fly smaller jets for the airline's American Eagle unit and their level of pay.

American wants to use lower-paid pilots from another union on the American Eagle regional flights, which the APA opposes. The airline, a unit of AMR Corp., wants lower costs to compete with other major airlines' regional commuter services.
Mayhew said the company's apparent rejection of the latest proposal involved the union's offer to have its pilots fly the American Eagle planes at what he called "competitive" wages.

Mayhew said the pilots also offered a new proposal on pay -- presumably less than the 11.5 percent pay increase over four years sought earlier -- but gave no details. The latest offer from American was a 6 percent raise over four years.
American Airlines Chairman Robert Crandall called for binding government arbitration of the dispute, a proposal the pilots have repeatedly rejected.
"I think mandatory binding arbitration should be required" to prevent airline strikes, Crandall told a congressional subcommittee.
"I seriously doubt we could accept that," union spokesman Wally Pitts said.
The two sides were already negotiating with a mediator present but binding arbitration would mean both parties agreed to abide by the decision of an arbitrator.
Crandall told a hearing of a House of Representatives Transportation subcommittee he was unsure if a strike could be avoided.
"We have two choices: we can either cave in or take a strike. A strike of 90 days will destroy this airline," he said.
As the talks entered their fourth day of intensive bargaining, President Bill Clinton was keeping a close watch.

Clinton could intervene and name an emergency board to try to resolve the issues. Creation of a board would prevent any work stoppages for 60 days while the board and the two parties again tried to mend their differences.
But at an unrelated news conference on Thursday, Clinton repeated that the parties should use the government mediator to reach an agreement.
